cards.explanation: The word is inexperienced. David tells the assembly that Solomon, his son and the king God chose, is “…young and inexperienced.” I think that's a dad being honest, not harsh. Nobody is born knowing how to build a temple, and I couldn't stamp a straight line my first day either.

The reason is that the palace is for the LORD God. David says, “The task is great because this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.” The size of the job comes from who it's for. Building for a neighbor is one thing, friends. Building for the LORD God is another level entirely.

The word is personal. David says he gives “…my personal treasures of gold and silver…” That's over and above all that he had provided for the temple. These are his own treasures, and he's the one giving them.

David gives because of his delight in the house of his God. He says it himself: “Moreover, because of my delight in the house of my God, I now give for it my personal treasures of gold and silver…” When you love something, friends, giving to it feels more like joy than a bill.

David asks who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today. His words are, “Now who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” He doesn't order anyone. He asks who is willing. After giving his own gold and silver, he opens the door for everyone else.

The answer is False. The leaders “gave willingly” (1 Chronicles 29:6), and the text says it plainly. David asked who was willing, and they stepped up. The people rejoiced because the leaders had given “…freely and wholeheartedly.” (1 Chronicles 29:9).

The word is rejoice. The text says, “…the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders…” They had given to the LORD “…freely and wholeheartedly.” and King David also rejoiced greatly. When giving comes from the heart, the whole room feels it. I can hop on my gold base just reading it.

The reason is that everything in heaven and on earth is the LORD's. David says it right in his prayer: “…for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You.” That's why the greatness, the power and the glory are the LORD's. When everything is already His, there's nothing left to compete with Him.

The answer is the LORD. David prays, “Both riches and honor come from You, and You are the ruler over all.” He's talking to the LORD, so the answer is right there in his prayer. Think about that, friends: this man had just handed over a mountain of gold, and he still says it all comes from God.

The answer is that everything comes from God's own hand. David answers his own question this way: “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.” They gave generously, but what they gave came from God's own hand. That's the whole secret.

The answer is the heart. David prays, “I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness.” God looks at the heart, not just what we hand over. That's why David talks about giving willingly and with an upright heart.

The answer is False. David tells God, “All these things I have given willingly and with an upright heart…” He also says he saw the people there giving “…joyfully and willingly to You.” No grudge anywhere in that prayer.

David asks the LORD to keep the same desire they just showed. His prayer is, “O LORD, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, keep this desire forever in the intentions of the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You.” The desire is the willing giving they had just shown. David wants it to last, and he asks God to point their hearts toward Him.

The word is build. David prays for Solomon, “…a whole heart to keep and carry out all Your commandments, decrees, and statutes, and to build Your palace for which I have made provision.” Building is the job David is praying about. David has made provision, and now he prays for Solomon's heart. A good dad does both.

The answer is True. The text says, “They bowed down and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.” The whole assembly blessed the LORD first, since David had told them to. Then they bowed to the LORD and to the king.

They anoint him as king. The text says, “Then, for a second time, they designated David’s son Solomon as king, anointing him before the LORD as ruler…” Solomon is David's son, and he's now the king. A second time means he'd been made king before, and this time it's out in the open with the whole assembly.
The name is Zadok. The text says they anointed Solomon “…as ruler, and Zadok as the priest.” Solomon is anointed as ruler, and Zadok is anointed as the priest. Two jobs, two people, one big day.

His reign begins with him prospering and all Israel obeying him. The text says, “So Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of his father David. He prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.” The reign begins with success and a whole nation behind him. It's a strong start for a king who was called young and inexperienced.

The answer is True. The text says, “All the officials and mighty men, as well as all of King David’s sons, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.” Even David's own sons were in on it. Nobody was left out of that line.

The answer is False. The LORD “…bestowed on him royal majesty such as had not been bestowed on any king in Israel before him.” It wasn't the same. Not a single king in Israel before him had been given what Solomon was given.

The word is Hebron. The text says David's reign was “…seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” That adds up to forty years, and I checked it twice with my mustache. Hebron came first, then Jerusalem.

David dies at a ripe old age, full of honor. The text says, “He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor, and his son Solomon reigned in his place.” It's a full life with a full finish. Years, riches and honor are the three things the text says he was full of.
